lead: Work crosses a boundary when a force moves through a distance. In a gas, the force comes from pressure on a moving piston. This is displacement work, also called boundary work or p dV work. It appears in engines, compressors and steam turbines. The same force × displacement pattern covers a spring, a charged capacitor and a liquid film. This chapter shows how to compute each from a path, how to read the sign, and why unit consistency decides the marks.
prereq: You need: 1.4 for quasi-static paths and 1.6 for the work sign convention.

sections.h3: Displacement work is the area under the p–V path

blocks.text: Displacement work is the work done when a boundary moves against pressure. Take a gas in a piston–cylinder as the system. Let p be the absolute pressure in pascal (Pa) and V the volume in cubic metre (m³). In a quasi-static process the pressure is uniform inside at every instant, and the path can be drawn on a p–V diagram. The work done by the system is the area under that path.
W = ∫ p dV  (from V₁ to V₂)
blocks.where: W is work done by the system in joule (J); p is absolute pressure in Pa; V is volume in m³; V₁ and V₂ are the initial and final volumes.

blocks.text: The area sign follows the direction. Expansion from left to right gives positive work by the system. Compression from right to left gives negative work by the system. A path that goes out and back encloses an area; the net work is the enclosed area with its sign. Work depends on the path, not only on the end states (see 1.3). For a constant-pressure process, p comes out of the integral: W = p(V₂ − V₁). If p is in kPa and V in m³, the answer is in kJ because 1 kPa × 1 m³ = 1 kJ.

Three non-flow work modes follow the force × displacement pattern. Spring or elastic work first. A spring with spring constant k, in N/m, is stretched from extension x₁ to x₂, in m. The work input to the spring is:

blocks.where: W is work input to the spring in J; k is the spring constant in N/m; x₁ and x₂ are the initial and final extensions in m. Work done by the spring is −W.

blocks.text: Electric work. Move charge dq through a potential difference φ. The work input is:

blocks.where: W is electric work input in J; φ is the electric potential difference in volt (V); q is charge in coulomb (C); dq is a small charge.

blocks.text: For a capacitor, q = Cφ, so charging from 0 to φ gives W = ½Cφ², where C is capacitance in farad (F). Surface-tension work. Stretch a liquid surface by dA at surface tension γ. The work input is:

blocks.where: W is surface-tension work input in J; γ is surface tension in N/m; A is surface area in m²; dA is a small area change.

blocks.text: For a soap film, A must include both surfaces, so a factor 2 appears. Magnetic work appears in some syllabi as a field–magnetisation integral; this chapter only needs recognition. Compression is not a separate formula: it is displacement work with V₂ < V₁ and a negative sign.

sections.h3: Signs, units and a safe method

blocks.text: Use this order in an exam.

items: Mark the system boundary and the process path.
Write p as a function of V, or note that p is constant.
Integrate from V₁ to V₂ for displacement work.
Attach the sign: expansion positive, compression negative.
Convert units before writing the final answer.

blocks.text: Table 1 lists the work modes. The area under a p–V line has units Pa × m³ = J. A common unit slip is p in kPa with V in m³; the number is then in kJ, not J. A second slip is using gauge pressure in p dV. Thermodynamic work uses absolute pressure. A third slip is treating the area of a closed loop as zero. A clockwise loop on a p–V diagram gives positive net work; an anticlockwise loop gives negative net work.

figure.caption: The horizontal line is a constant-pressure path at 200 kPa from 0.10 m³ to 0.25 m³. The area under it is 30 kJ, the displacement work.

spec.aria: A plot of pressure against volume shows a horizontal line at 200 kPa from volume 0.10 to 0.25 m³; the area under it is the displacement work.

examples.question: A gas expands quasi-statically at constant pressure 200 kPa from V₁ = 0.10 m³ to V₂ = 0.25 m³. Find the displacement work W = ∫ p dV and state its sign.
steps: Identify the path: p = 200 kPa at every state, so p is constant.
Write the integral: W = ∫ p dV from V₁ to V₂.
Take p outside: W = p(V₂ − V₁).
Convert: 1 kPa·m³ = 1 kJ, so W = 30 kJ.
Sign: volume increases, so the gas does work on the surroundings; W is positive.
examples.answer: W = +30 kJ; work is done by the system.

traps: Using p in kPa and V in m³ and calling the result joule. 200 kPa × 0.15 m³ = 30 kJ, not 30 J.
Using gauge pressure instead of absolute pressure in ∫ p dV. Absolute pressure is required.
For compression, writing a positive number because the arithmetic is positive. p dV is negative when V falls; work done by the system is negative.
Treating W = p(V₂ − V₁) as valid for every process. It is valid only when p is constant.
Forgetting that a soap film has two surfaces when using W = ∫ γ dA; use total area.

quiz.q: Define displacement work for a quasi-static process.
quiz.a: W = ∫ p dV from V₁ to V₂, the area under the p–V path; p is absolute pressure and V is volume.

quiz.q: Why does work depend on the path in a p–V diagram?
quiz.a: Different paths between the same two states enclose different areas under the curve. Work is that area, so it depends on path, unlike a property change.

quiz.q: A gas is compressed at constant 150 kPa from 0.40 m³ to 0.25 m³. Find W by the system.
quiz.a: W = 150(0.25 − 0.40) = −22.5 kPa·m³ = −22.5 kJ. The negative sign means work is done on the system.

quiz.q: A gas expands at 200 kPa from 0.10 to 0.25 m³, then is compressed back at 100 kPa from 0.25 to 0.10 m³. Find net work and explain the sign from the loop direction.
quiz.a: Expansion: W₁ = 200 × 0.15 = 30 kJ. Compression: W₂ = 100 × (0.10 − 0.25) = −15 kJ. Net W = 15 kJ. A clockwise loop gives positive net work by the system.

quiz.q: A spring with k = 400 N/m is stretched from x = 0.10 m to x = 0.20 m. Find work input to the spring.
State the units of γ and k in surface-tension and spring work.
quiz.a: γ is in N/m; k is in N/m.

quiz.q: Why is gauge pressure not used in p dV?
quiz.a: p dV uses absolute pressure because the force on the piston comes from absolute pressure. Gauge pressure omits atmospheric pressure and gives wrong work.

quiz.q: A capacitor is charged from 0 to V. Explain why W = ∫ V dq gives ½CV², not CV².
quiz.a: The potential V rises as q rises. The average potential is V/2, so W = ½CV². Using CV² assumes the final V acts for the whole charge.

beyond: Not for the exam. Displacement work is the accounting basis for compressor and engine indicator diagrams in industry. Spring and electric work appear in actuator and capacitor design, and surface-tension work appears in microfluidic devices and solder joint formation. A next search is 'indicator diagram area' and 'generalised force displacement work'. Magnetic work leads into thermodynamics of magnetic materials.
